issues.legal_issue: Evidence from witnesses related to the deceased may be relied on to support a conviction when careful scrutiny shows it to be credible.
material_facts: The four eyewitnesses were related to the deceased or to members of the deceased’s family.
The courts found that the witnesses had seen the occurrence and that their accounts were clear, cogent, and credible after careful scrutiny.
The eyewitness accounts were corroborated by the medical evidence.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship to the deceased did not make their evidence inadmissible or unreliable, and their credible testimony could be relied on without corroboration as a matter of law.
issues.legal_principle: Relationship to the deceased does not by itself discredit a witness or require corroboration as a rule of law. The evidence of a related or interested witness must be scrutinized carefully as a rule of prudence; if it is consistent, truthful, and credible, it may be relied on. The Court relied on Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, (1976) 4 SCC 369; Balraje alias Trimbak v. State of Maharashtra, (2010) 6 SCC 673; Prahalad Patel v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2011) 4 SCC 262; Israr v. State of U.P., (2005) 9 SCC 616; S. Sudershan Reddy v. State of A.P., (2006) 10 SCC 163; State of U.P. v. Naresh, (2011) 4 SCC 324; Jarnail Singh v. State of Punjab, (2009) 9 SCC 719; and Vishnu v. State of Rajasthan, (2009) 10 SCC 477.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the court must decide whether the accused committed the charged offence.
predicates.witness_related: A witness who gives evidence about the alleged offence is related to the deceased or complainant.
predicates.testimony_cogent_credible: After careful scrutiny, the witness’s account is found to be clear, consistent, truthful, and credible.

issues.definition: When a criminal case includes credible testimony from a witness related to the deceased or complainant, that testimony may support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Minor contradictions in witnesses’ accounts do not require rejection of the prosecution evidence when they do not undermine its material parts.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses differed in some descriptions of the weapons used and the injuries caused, and there were omissions or discrepancies between their police statements and testimony.
The courts found those differences minor and not directed to the principal acts attributed to the accused.
The witnesses gave statements soon after the incident, their testimony was recorded later, and the principal account was supported by medical evidence.
issues.conclusion: The minor contradictions did not justify rejecting the eyewitness testimony or overturning the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: A court should sift evidence cautiously to separate truth from falsehood, exaggeration, and embellishment; discrepancies do not require discarding the whole prosecution case unless they undermine its substratum or a material part of the evidence. The rule falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a sound rule. The Court relied on Gurbachan Singh v. Satpal Singh, (1990) 1 SCC 445, and Sohrab s/o Beli Nayata v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1972) 3 SCC 751.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the court must decide whether the accused committed the charged offence.
predicates.contradictions_minor: The witnesses differ on details, but the differences do not concern a material part of the prosecution account.
predicates.core_account_consistent: The witnesses consistently describe the principal occurrence and the material acts attributed to the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, minor contradictions do not require rejection of testimony when the witnesses consistently describe the material occurrence and acts.

issues.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly may be held liable for an offence committed in prosecution of its common object even if no weapon is recovered personally from that member, where the evidence establishes participation and the required common object and knowledge.
material_facts: The accused was charged as a member of an unlawful assembly and was identified by eyewitnesses as participating in the group attack, including by striking a victim with an iron pipe.
The attack involved multiple blows with weapons, caused fatal injuries, and the evidence supported the finding that the assembly’s common object was to cause the victims’ deaths.
A weapon was not recovered personally from that accused, but the iron pipe was recovered from another accused’s house and weapons were recovered from other members of the group.
The trial court found the accused guilty as a member of the unlawful assembly, and the Supreme Court accepted the eyewitness and medical evidence implicating him.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a weapon recovery from the accused did not prevent his conviction; the evidence supported his liability as a member of the unlawful assembly.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, a court must make a clear finding about the nature and unlawful character of the assembly’s common object. The evidence must show that the offence was committed in prosecution of that object and that the other members knew or were aware that the offence was likely to be committed in its prosecution. Individual weapon recovery is not essential where the evidence otherwise establishes participation and the requirements for liability as a member of the assembly.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_case and accused_identified_as_participant and common_object_death and offense_likelihood_known_to_members and group_attack_evidence

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The prosecution alleges that the accused is liable for an offence as a member of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_identified_as_participant: Evidence identifies the accused as participating in the group’s criminal conduct.
predicates.common_object_death: The evidence establishes that the assembly had the common object of causing death.
predicates.offense_likelihood_known_to_members: The evidence establishes that the members knew or were aware that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object.
predicates.group_attack_evidence: Evidence of the group’s weapons, acts, or resulting injuries supports the account of the accused’s participation in the attack.

issues.definition: In an unlawful-assembly case, participation supported by evidence, a common object to cause death, and members’ awareness that the offence was likely mean that the lack of a personal weapon recovery does not defeat member liability.

issues.legal_issue: Interference with concurrent criminal convictions is unwarranted in a special leave appeal when the evidence supports the findings and no material error is shown.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused, and the High Court affirmed the convictions on appeal.
The Supreme Court found the eyewitness evidence acceptable, the contradictions trivial, and the medical evidence corroborative.
The Supreme Court found no error, infirmity, or valid legal ground warranting interference.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India and held that interference was not warranted on the record before it, which disclosed no error, infirmity, or valid legal ground for disturbing the concurrent findings.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a special leave appeal challenging criminal convictions affirmed by an appellate court.
predicates.concurrent_findings_supported_by_credibl: The trial and appellate courts’ material findings are supported by evidence found credible on review.
predicates.no_material_error_shown: The appeal does not establish a material error, infirmity, or valid legal ground for disturbing the findings.

issues.definition: When a special leave appeal challenges criminal convictions affirmed by an appellate court, credible evidentiary support and no shown material error mean that Supreme Court interference is unwarranted.
